passages.text: Honeybees convey the location of food through a remarkably Ⓐ<u>economical</u> behavior known as the waggle dance. A forager returning to the hive performs a series of movements whose direction Ⓑ<u>encodes</u> the angle between the food source and the sun, and the duration of each waggle run conveys distance: the longer the run, the Ⓒ<u>farther</u> away the flowers. Other bees press their antennae against her body to pick up the scent of the blossoms she has visited, and as she circles they follow her closely. The system is so precise that recruits can pinpoint a patch of flowers several kilometers from the colony. Even more strikingly, the dance remains Ⓓ<u>intelligible</u> inside the pitch-dark hive, where bees rely on touch and vibration rather than Ⓔ<u>scent</u>, an elegant solution to a problem that might baffle many engineers.

When prices rise steadily, money lying Ⓐ<u>idle</u> in a bank account gradually loses its purchasing power. A savings account paying 2 percent interest during a year of 5 percent inflation leaves the saver Ⓑ<u>poorer</u> in real terms, even though the balance on the statement has grown. For this reason financial advisers often exhort households to move their savings into assets that tend to Ⓒ<u>lag behind</u> prices. But inflation does not afflict everyone equally: borrowers with fixed-rate loans may actually benefit by repaying their debts with money worth less than at the time of borrowing. Lenders, by contrast, watch the real value of their repayments Ⓓ<u>erode</u>. This Ⓔ<u>lopsided</u> distribution of gains and losses explains why inflation is as much a political issue as an economic one, pitting debtors against creditors.

Physicians have long recognized that a patient's beliefs can shape the course of an illness, and the placebo effect offers the most Ⓐ<u>striking</u> evidence of this power of expectation. In clinical trials, patients given sugar pills Ⓑ<u>routinely</u> improve, sometimes almost as much as those who receive the real drug. Many report substantial relief from pain, Ⓒ<u>provided</u> they believe the pills are genuine medicine. Researchers suspect that the ritual of treatment itself Ⓓ<u>elicits</u> the body's own healing responses. Yet the effect has clear limits: placebos can alleviate subjective symptoms such as pain and nausea, but they cannot shrink tumors or cure infections. Physicians therefore regard the placebo effect as a Ⓔ<u>substitute for</u> real treatment rather than a complement to it, a reminder that how care is delivered matters as well as what is delivered.

Discussions of fashion's environmental footprint tend to fasten on production: the water consumed to grow cotton, the dyes released into rivers, the microscopic plastic fibers that synthetic fabrics shed in every wash. These costs are real, and they remain largely invisible to the shopper at the till. Yet a growing body of life-cycle research suggests that the single most consequential variable is not how a garment is made but how long it is worn. Extending the active life of clothing by a few months, by some estimates, does more to shrink its footprint than any improvement in fibers or factories now on the horizon.
From this it is tempting to conclude that the burden lies squarely with consumers, who need only buy less and mend more. Critics of this view have a point. Exhorting individuals to show restraint, they argue, conveniently relieves retailers of responsibility for a business model built on releasing new designs every few weeks; and the advice to buy fewer, better-made pieces presumes a budget that many households do not have. A coat that lasts a decade is a bargain only for those who can afford its price today. On this account, the problem is structural, and appeals to personal virtue are at best a distraction.
Still, the structural critique proves less than it seems to. That a habit is encouraged by an industry does not make it immune to change, and durability is not solely a matter of price: much discarded clothing is thrown away not because it has worn out but because it no longer pleases its owner. Regulating production and changing how we regard what we already own are therefore not rival remedies. The first may determine how much harm each garment carries into the world; only the second determines how many garments we need.

Imagine being offered a bet on a coin toss: heads, you win $110; tails, you lose $100. Although the wager favors you on average, most people decline it. For several decades behavioral economists have treated such refusals as evidence of loss aversion, the tendency to feel a loss roughly twice as keenly as an equivalent gain. The idea has proved remarkably fertile. It has been invoked to explain why investors cling to falling stocks, why shoppers resent a surcharge more than they welcome an equal discount, and why marketers so often tell customers what they stand to lose rather than what they might gain.
A number of researchers now contend that the principle has been stretched too far. When the sums at stake are small, they point out, many people show little or no asymmetry, and some experiments that seemed to reveal loss aversion can be explained by other factors, such as distrust of the person offering the bet or a reluctance to depart from the status quo. If losses truly loomed larger in every case, the critics ask, why does the effect fade so readily when the same choice is described differently?
These objections deserve a hearing, but they do not amount to a refutation. That an effect depends on context is not evidence that it is illusory; few findings in psychology hold regardless of circumstance. What the critiques do undermine is the habit of treating loss aversion as a fixed constant of human nature, a universal ratio that can be plugged into any model. The more defensible claim is narrower: when people perceive an outcome as a loss relative to what they expected or already possess, and when the stakes matter to them, losses tend to weigh more heavily than gains. That claim is less dramatic, but it is also more likely to survive the next round of experiments.

Octopuses are among the most intelligent invertebrates. In laboratories they solve puzzles, unscrew the lids of jars, and occasionally escape from their tanks at night with no keeper watching. Unlike humans, they carry most of their neurons in their arms rather than in a central brain, so each arm can touch, taste, and react with a surprising degree of autonomy. Octopuses can also alter the color and texture of their skin in a fraction of a second to blend into their surroundings, yet most species are paradoxically thought to be color-blind; how they match hues they apparently cannot see remains an enigma. Their abilities are all the more striking given their brief lives: most species live only one or two years.

The sociologist Robert Merton observed that eminent scientists tend to receive disproportionate credit for work comparable to that of lesser-known colleagues. When two researchers independently publish similar findings, the more famous is cited more often; when a paper has several authors, readers remember the most prominent name. Merton called this pattern the Matthew effect, after the verse in the Gospel of Matthew about how those who have shall receive still more. Because recognition brings funding, students, and attention, each of which makes further recognition more likely, the advantage compounds over a career.
It would be easy to read this as a simple story of injustice, and some commentators do. Yet Merton himself saw a functional side to the pattern. Faced with far more papers than anyone could read, scientists need some way of deciding where to direct their attention, and a track record is not a foolish guide: a researcher who has been right before is, other things being equal, somewhat more likely to be right again. On this view, the extra credit flowing to famous names is less a reward for status than a rough proxy for reliability.
The argument is sound as far as it goes, but it goes less far than its defenders suppose. A shortcut that is reasonable for each individual reader can still produce a distorted result when everyone takes it at once. If every reader favors the familiar name, the unknown researcher's identical finding is not merely discounted but may never be read at all, and the track record that might have earned her a hearing is never allowed to form. The efficiency of the shortcut, in other words, is purchased partly at the expense of those whom it renders invisible, and that cost falls hardest on the young.

For most of the digital age, lawmakers treated software as something to be regulated only after it had caused harm. The rapid proliferation of generative artificial intelligence has unsettled that habit. In 2024 the European Union adopted a sweeping law that sorts AI systems according to the risk they pose. Applications judged to carry an unacceptable risk, such as government "social scoring" of citizens, are prohibited outright; those used in sensitive areas such as hiring, credit, and policing must meet stringent standards of transparency and human oversight; and the vast majority, from spam filters to video-game characters, face few obligations at all.
Supporters regard this graduated approach as a judicious compromise. Rather than smothering an entire technology, it concentrates scrutiny where the stakes for individuals are highest, much as societies already regulate medicines more strictly than breakfast cereals. Critics on one side contend that the rules are too lax, leaving powerful general-purpose models largely to police themselves. Critics on the other side warn that the cost of compliance will fall hardest on small start-ups without legions of lawyers and may ____ the very innovation that Europe hopes to foster.
Other governments have watched closely, and some have preferred voluntary guidelines, fearing that binding rules would drive investment elsewhere; others have begun drafting laws of their own. As AI products cross borders effortlessly, a company that wishes to sell in Europe may find it simpler to adopt European standards everywhere than to maintain separate versions for each market. Then the law could <u>punch above its weight</u>, shaping the technology far beyond the continent where it was written.

In 2025 the United States raised import duties on a scale not seen in nearly a century, and trading partners from Canada to China retaliated swiftly with measures of their own. Proponents advanced several arguments for the new tariffs. The tariffs would revive domestic manufacturing, curtail dependence on rival powers for critical goods, and give negotiators leverage to extract concessions from other countries.
Most economists remain skeptical. The reason lies in a question that sounds deceptively simple: who actually pays? A tariff is collected from the domestic company that imports the goods, not from the foreign exporter. That company can absorb the cost, eroding its own profits; it can pressure suppliers abroad to cut their prices; or it can simply pass the cost on to its customers. Studies of earlier rounds of tariffs found that <u>the third option</u> largely prevailed, leaving the burden mainly on domestic importers and the households that buy from them. In this sense a tariff functions much like a sales tax, but one rarely shown as a separate line on a receipt.
History offers a further caution: the Smoot-Hawley Tariff of 1930 was meant to insulate American farmers and factories but provoked retaliation abroad and coincided with a collapse in world trade that exacerbated the Great Depression. Few economists blame the tariff alone for the slump, but the episode is routinely cited as a lesson in how protection can invite reprisal.
Defenders reply that comparisons with the 1930s are overdrawn, and that some loss of efficiency is a price worth paying for secure supply chains. The dispute, in short, is less about arithmetic than about what a nation chooses to value.

Does the language we speak shape the way we think? The strongest form of this idea is often associated with the linguist Benjamin Lee Whorf. It holds that language determines thought and that speakers of different languages inhabit different mental worlds, a view that few researchers today would countenance. If language truly imprisoned thought, translating between languages or grasping a concept without a word in one's own language would be impossible, yet people do both easily all the time.
A weaker version of the idea, however, has garnered considerable support. Speakers of languages that use compass directions for locations, placing a cup north of a plate rather than to its left, turn out to be remarkably adept at keeping track of their orientation even inside unfamiliar buildings. Speakers of languages with separate basic words for light blue and dark blue discern those shades slightly faster than other speakers. In such cases, language does not create an ability out of nothing, but it seems to ____ certain habits of attention, much as a daily route through a city makes some streets more familiar than others.
Even these modest findings have proved contentious. Some celebrated claims have proved difficult for other laboratories to replicate, such as the suggestion that the grammatical gender of a noun colors how speakers describe objects like bridges or keys. Skeptics also caution that cultural practices rather than language itself may account for many of the observed differences. The emerging consensus is a cautious one: language is one influence on thought among many, not its master.

My grandfather repaired watches for fifty years in a shop so narrow that two customers could not stand side by side. When I was twelve, I spent a summer there, mostly sweeping the floor and sorting minuscule screws into labeled tins. I was bored. I made sure he knew it, sighing loudly whenever he asked me to fetch something. One sweltering afternoon he handed me a pocket watch that had stopped and told me, without further instruction, to find out why. I opened the case and stared at a tangle of gears, springs, and jewels so small that my breath seemed to stir them. For an hour I found nothing, and my exasperation slowly gave way to obstinacy. Then, just as I was about to give up, I noticed a single hair caught between two wheels. I removed it with a pair of tweezers while my hands quivered slightly, and when I closed the case, the watch began to tick again.
I expected praise, perhaps even a small reward. Instead my grandfather simply nodded, as if nothing remarkable had happened, and handed me another watch from the drawer. Only years later did I understand what he had given me that afternoon. It was not a lesson about watches, which I never learned to repair, but about attention: the patience to keep looking after the obvious explanations have been exhausted. When I became a doctor, I found myself returning to that narrow shop in my mind whenever a patient's symptoms refused to make sense. Somewhere, I would tell myself, <u>there is a hair caught between the wheels</u>.

For years as a primary-school teacher, I praised my pupils for being smart, believing that such praise built confidence. Research on motivation eventually persuaded me that this well-meant habit could backfire. In a widely cited series of experiments, children praised for their intelligence after solving puzzles were more likely to choose easy tasks afterward, apparently to protect their image as clever, whereas children praised for their effort tended to seek out harder problems and persist longer. The explanation offered was that praise teaches children what ability is: praise for intelligence implies a fixed trait, so failure becomes a verdict; praise for effort implies that ability can grow, so failure becomes information.
The idea spread with remarkable speed, and schools around the world adopted programs to instill this "growth mindset." It would be convenient to report that the programs delivered what the experiments seemed to promise. They did not, at least not uniformly. Large trials have found average effects that are real but small, concentrated among struggling students and nearly absent among those already doing well. Some researchers have gone further, suggesting that the original findings were inflated by the enthusiasm of those who produced them. And teachers who praised effort indiscriminately, applauding a child's hard work even when nothing had been learned, found that the praise soon rang hollow.
None of this, I think, returns us to where I began. A modest effect is not the same as no effect, and the critics' strongest point concerns not the insight itself but the hope that a few lessons on mindset could transform achievement on their own. What the research left me with is something more ____ than a technique: an awareness that whatever adults choose to praise sends a quiet but persistent message about what they value, and that children hear the message long after the praise itself is forgotten.

In 2014 the Court of Justice of the European Union ruled that individuals could ask search engines to remove links to information about them that was inadequate, irrelevant, or no longer relevant. The case had been brought by a Spanish man. A search for his name still produced a newspaper notice from years earlier about the forced sale of his property to pay long-settled debts. The ruling established what has come to be called the right to be forgotten.
Supporters welcomed the decision because it answered a genuinely new problem: before the internet, old newspaper stories receded from public view as they were filed away in archives; today, a single search can bring a person's worst moment back to the surface decades later. Without some way to limit this, they argue, people could never truly move on from their mistakes.
Critics, particularly in the United States, saw the ruling as a threat to free expression. In their view it forced private companies to decide case by case what the public has a right to know, a role belonging to courts and editors, not search engines. They also warned that the powerful could exploit the right to bury information that is embarrassing but genuinely ____ to the public, such as a politician's past business dealings.
Notably the ruling did not require the original newspaper to delete anything. The article remained available, although it became harder to find through a search for the man's name. The court thus sought to curb how easily information could be found, not its existence.

For generations home insurance has functioned as a quiet form of solidarity: many households pay modest premiums so that the few struck by fire or flood can rebuild. The arrangement depends on disasters being rare and roughly predictable, and a warming climate is eroding both conditions. Several large insurers have stopped writing new homeowners' policies in parts of California, citing wildfire risk and spiraling construction costs, while a number of smaller companies in Florida have collapsed or withdrawn after costly hurricane seasons.
Where private insurers retreat, state-backed programs typically step in as insurers of last resort, offering more limited coverage at premiums held below what the risk would warrant. Economists are, for the most part, unenthusiastic. Such programs, they argue, merely <u>paper over the cracks</u>: a premium that reflects risk tells homeowners, builders, and local governments where it is imprudent to build, and rewards those who invest in fire-resistant roofs or flood defenses. Suppress that price, and people will go on building in places that are growing more dangerous every year.
The argument is compelling in the abstract, and it is hard to fault as a guide to where new homes should go. It is less persuasive as an account of what is owed to those already there. The households facing the steepest increases are frequently those least able to move: retirees on fixed incomes, families whose wealth is tied up in a house that may soon be unsellable. To let the price signal fall on them at full strength is to ask the people who made the least consequential decisions to bear the largest share of the adjustment.
None of this vindicates open-ended subsidies, which would merely postpone the reckoning while enlarging it. It suggests rather that help should be aimed at existing residents and tied to measures that reduce risk, while new construction faces the full price. Adapting to a hotter world will require deciding not only how to share the costs of disaster but who should ultimately bear them.

When photography was introduced in 1839, some painters predicted the end of their art, since a machine could now record a face or a landscape with a precision no brush could rival. For miniature portraitists the fear proved justified: cheap photographic portraits took over their market within a few decades. Yet the more familiar story holds that photography, far from killing painting, liberated it. Relieved of the duty to record appearances, painters turned to what a camera could not capture, such as the play of light at a given moment, the emotional charge of color, and the inner experience of seeing, and Impressionism was the result.
The story is attractive, and it has the further merit of consoling anyone who fears that a new technology will render an old art obsolete. Historians of art have nonetheless grown wary of it. Painters had been experimenting with loose brushwork and fleeting effects of light well before 1839, and academic realism did not wither when the camera arrived; it flourished in the salons for another half-century. If photography freed painting from the burden of exact reproduction, it is curious how many painters declined to be freed. Some even borrowed from the camera, adopting the unorthodox cropping and frozen motion of snapshots, which suggests that the new medium served as a source of ideas as much as a rival.
These objections complicate the liberation story without quite overturning it. Photography did not invent the impulses that produced Impressionism, but it altered the conditions under which they were judged. Once exact likeness had become ____, a painter who pursued it competed with a machine, while one who pursued something else no longer seemed merely unskilled. The camera, in other words, did less to change what painters wanted to do than to change what their choices meant. The pattern may be general: a new technology seldom dictates the direction an older art will take, but it can redraw the map on which that direction is read.

South Korea has become the starkest example of a demographic shift now spreading across wealthy nations. The total fertility rate is the average number of children a woman is expected to have over her lifetime. South Korea's rate fell to 0.72 in 2023, roughly a third of the 2.1 needed to keep a population stable without immigration. A slight rebound to 0.75 the following year was greeted with relief, but few demographers regard it as the start of a durable reversal.
Successive governments have spent lavishly on the problem, offering cash payments at birth, monthly child allowances, and subsidized childcare. Measured against the scale of the decline, the results have been <u>a drop in the bucket</u>. Surveys suggest why: young adults cite the cost of housing, cutthroat competition over education, and long working hours far more often than a shortage of public money as reasons for delaying or forgoing children. Women in particular describe a harsh ____ between career and motherhood. Taking leave can stall a promotion for years, and household duties remain unevenly shared.
The consequences extend well beyond the maternity ward, since a shrinking workforce must support a burgeoning population of retirees, straining pension funds and health systems. Rural schools are closing for lack of pupils. The armed forces face a dwindling pool of conscripts.
Few societies have managed to raise birth rates substantially. Some analysts therefore argue that the goal should shift to adapting to a smaller population through automation, later retirement, and immigration. Others insist on tackling the underlying impediments, from housing to workplace culture, for their own sake.

Despite its name, the Bayeux Tapestry is not a tapestry. A true tapestry has its design Ⓐ<u>woven</u> into the fabric on a loom, whereas the famous work in Normandy is an embroidery stitched in colored wool onto long strips of linen. Roughly seventy meters long, it narrates the Norman conquest of England in 1066, culminating at Hastings. Its scenes are remarkably Ⓑ<u>static</u>: soldiers tumble from horses, ships are laden with weapons and wine, and a comet blazes ominously overhead. Historians prize it as a Ⓒ<u>rare</u> visual record of eleventh-century life. Yet they also treat it with Ⓓ<u>caution</u>, because it was almost certainly made for the victors and tells the story from their perspective. Like many official histories, it is as Ⓔ<u>partisan</u> as it is beautiful, a work of persuasion disguised as a chronicle.

Why do people sometimes fail to help in an emergency when many others are present? In classic experiments in the late 1960s, John Darley and Bibb Latané found that the presence of other bystanders Ⓐ<u>reduced</u> the likelihood that any one person would intervene. Part of the reason is that people look to others to Ⓑ<u>construe</u> an ambiguous situation, and if everyone appears calm, each Ⓒ<u>infers</u> that nothing is wrong. In one study, participants completing questionnaires in a room slowly filling with smoke were far more likely to report it when alone than when seated with others who remained Ⓓ<u>impassive</u>. Responsibility is also diffused: when many could act, each feels less obliged to do so. Awareness may help. Singling out one person in a crowd and asking directly for help can Ⓔ<u>compound</u> the paralysis.

Twice a day, along most coasts, the sea creeps up the shore and recedes. The chief cause is the Moon's gravity, which pulls Ⓐ<u>more</u> strongly on the side of the Earth facing it than on the far side. This difference stretches the oceans into two bulges, one facing the Moon and one on the far side, and the rotating Earth carries coastlines through both. The Sun exerts a similar but Ⓑ<u>weaker</u> influence, because it is far more distant, despite its vastly greater mass. At new and full moon the Sun and Moon line up, and their effects Ⓒ<u>alternate</u> to produce especially high and low tides, known as spring tides. During the quarter moons they pull at right angles, so their effects partly Ⓓ<u>offset</u> each other and the tidal range dwindles. Local geography can Ⓔ<u>amplify</u> these patterns dramatically.

Why do I cherish the wobbly bookshelf I assembled myself more than the sturdier one I bought ready-made? Behavioral economists have a name for this tendency: the IKEA effect, after the retailer whose furniture arrives flat-packed. In a series of studies, people who folded origami figures or built simple storage boxes were willing to pay considerably more for their own creations than for identical items made by others, and they assumed, wrongly, that strangers would value them just as highly.
It is tempting to dismiss all this as vanity. On this view, people inflate the worth of their handiwork for the same reason they defend a bad investment: having poured in time and effort, they cannot bear to admit that the result is ordinary. There is something to this. The overvaluation is real, and the builders' confidence that others would share it suggests a blind spot rather than a sober judgment.
Yet the vanity account struggles with a detail that the researchers took pains to document. When participants built something and then dismantled it, or were stopped before they could finish, the extra attachment largely vanished, even though they had invested nearly as much effort. If sunk effort alone explained the effect, an unfinished box should have been cherished almost as much as a completed one. What seems to matter is not labor as such but labor that ends in visible success, the sense of having made something that works.
This suggests a more modest conclusion than either enthusiasts or cynics tend to draw. Effort does not automatically confer value, and the affection it breeds is not entirely rational. But neither is it mere self-flattery. It may be better understood as a reward for competence, which would explain why designers who ask customers to contribute a little work can sell them more than a product, provided the work is not so difficult that customers fail.

In the 1920s and early 1930s, researchers at the Hawthorne Works, a large electrical factory near Chicago, set out to discover how working conditions affected productivity. In the best-known tests they raised and lowered the lighting in a workroom, and output seemed to rise almost regardless of the change. The explanation that eventually prevailed was that the workers were responding not to the lights but to the attention: knowing they were being studied, they worked harder. Under the name "the Hawthorne effect," this idea entered textbooks as a standing warning that observation can alter the behavior it seeks to measure.
Later scholars who returned to the surviving records were less impressed. The illumination studies were never properly written up, the groups were tiny, and output in the plant tended to rise anyway as the seasons changed. When economists reanalyzed data from a later phase of the research, they found little of the dramatic pattern the legend describes. Some critics have gone further and declared the Hawthorne effect a myth, a story that survived because it was too useful to abandon.
That verdict is understandable but too sweeping. The weakness of the Hawthorne evidence tells us that this particular factory is a poor foundation for the idea; it does not tell us that people never behave differently when watched. Researchers in medicine and education routinely find that participants who know they are being monitored change their habits, if usually less than the legend implies and not always in the same direction.
The lesson, then, is double. The name has outlived its evidence, and textbooks that cite Hawthorne as proof deserve correction. But the caution the name came to stand for remains sound, provided it is treated as a hypothesis to be tested in each study rather than a law that can simply be assumed.

Tardigrades, often called water bears, are microscopic animals that rarely grow longer than about a millimeter. Magnified, they resemble plump, eight-legged caterpillars lumbering through films of water on moss. In recent years they have become minor celebrities, hailed in headlines as the toughest animals on Earth, creatures that could outlast the end of the world.
The reputation is not baseless. When their surroundings dry out, many species expel nearly all the water from their bodies, curl into a shriveled state known as a tun, and suspend their metabolism almost entirely. In this condition they have survived temperatures close to absolute zero, doses of radiation hundreds of times what would kill a human, and, in one experiment, ten days of exposure to the vacuum of space, reviving when water returned.
But the headlines blur a distinction that biologists consider essential. These feats belong to the tun, not to the animal going about its life. An active tardigrade, swimming and feeding in its film of water, is about as fragile as other creatures its size, and even tuns do not survive every ordeal: in the space experiment, animals exposed to unfiltered solar radiation as well as the vacuum fared far worse. To call tardigrades indestructible is therefore to mistake a strategy of suspension for a strategy of resistance.
The distinction matters because it changes the question worth asking. If water bears simply possessed bodies of unusual toughness, the interesting puzzle would be their armor. Since they instead survive by shutting down, the puzzle becomes how a living system can stop almost completely and then start again, a question with implications for preserving vaccines, cells, and perhaps one day human tissues. Their resilience, in short, is a talent for waiting out bad times, not for thriving in them.

Why do songs that irritated me on first hearing so often become favorites after a few weeks on the radio? In the late 1960s the psychologist Robert Zajonc reported experiments suggesting an answer. Participants were shown unfamiliar stimuli, such as nonsense words or Chinese characters they could not read, some many times and others only once or twice. Asked later how much they liked each item, they consistently preferred the ones they had seen more often, even though they could not say what any of them meant. Zajonc called this the mere exposure effect.
The finding seems to overturn the proverb that familiarity breeds contempt, and it has been eagerly taken up by advertisers, who conclude that repetition is the surest route to affection. That conclusion goes well beyond the evidence. The effect is strongest for stimuli that people initially regard as neutral; repeating something they already dislike can deepen their aversion. It also tends to level off after a modest number of exposures, and endless repetition eventually breeds tedium, which is one reason advertisers rotate their commercials.
Nor is it clear why the effect occurs. One proposal is that familiar things feel safe: an organism that has met something repeatedly without harm has some reason to approach it. Another is that familiar stimuli are simply easier to process, and people mistake that ease for liking. The second account helps explain a striking later result: the effect can appear even when images are flashed too briefly to be consciously recognized, so that participants come to prefer items they do not remember having seen.
The proverb, then, is not so much refuted as qualified. Familiarity tends to breed a mild fondness for what was neutral, and contempt for what was already resented. My radio favorites may simply be the songs I disliked only a little.

Commentators dubbed 2024 the biggest election year in history: countries with roughly half of the world's population held national votes, from India and Indonesia to Mexico, the United Kingdom, and the United States. It was also the first such year in which persuasive fake audio and video could be produced cheaply by almost anyone with a laptop. Early in the year an automated telephone message imitating the voice of the American president exhorted voters in New Hampshire to skip a primary election, and fabricated clips of candidates circulated in several other countries.
Many observers braced for chaos, but in the event, a number of post-election reviews concluded that deepfakes had done less to sway results than feared. Most fabricated clips were quickly debunked, and those that spread widely tended to reach partisans whose minds were already made up. But researchers cautioned that this relative calm should not be mistaken for safety. A single well-timed forgery released hours before polls open may leave no time for ____.
Moreover the greatest damage may be indirect. Once the public knows that any recording can be forged, politicians caught on tape saying something embarrassing gain a convenient alibi: they can simply claim that the evidence is fake, a tactic legal scholars call <u>the liar's dividend</u>. Its corrosive effect does not depend on any particular forgery succeeding. It depends only on a pervasive atmosphere of doubt. Some experts therefore argue that technical fixes such as labeling machine-generated content must be accompanied by efforts to bolster trusted sources of news. Citizens will then still have somewhere to turn when they can no longer believe their own eyes.

Across the developed world, people are living longer and having fewer children, and the arithmetic of retirement is shifting accordingly. When many pension systems were designed, a worker retiring at sixty could expect to draw benefits for a decade or so; today that period often exceeds twenty years, while the number of workers contributing for each retiree steadily declines. The remedy most governments now favor is to keep people working longer. France raised its minimum pension age from 62 to 64 in 2023 despite months of protests, and in South Korea a debate over extending the legal retirement age from sixty to sixty-five has intensified.
The case for doing so is strong on its face. Today's sixty-year-olds are healthier and better educated than any previous generation of that age, and many want or need to keep earning. Retaining seasoned employees, advocates add, can ease labor shortages and preserve skills that take decades to acquire.
The objections deserve more weight than advocates usually give them. A lawyer may welcome a few extra years at her desk, but a construction worker whose body is worn out by fifty-five may experience <u>the same reform</u> as a cut in benefits rather than an opportunity. And in firms where pay rises automatically with seniority, older employees are expensive to keep, so young job seekers fear that longer tenure will ____ the openings available to graduates. Whether that fear is justified is disputed: studies in several countries find little evidence that older workers crowd out younger ones across the economy as a whole, though the effect may be real in particular firms with rigid pay scales.
None of this makes a later retirement age a mistake. It suggests rather that the policy is only as fair as the arrangements around it: pay tied to role rather than years of service, routes to gradual retirement, and provisions for those whose work wears out the body first.

Generative AI systems learn to write and draw by analyzing enormous quantities of text and images, much of it copied from the open web without the permission of those who created it. For several years this practice attracted scant legal scrutiny, but that changed as the systems became commercially lucrative. Since 2023 novelists, illustrators, photo agencies, music publishers, and a major American newspaper have filed lawsuits against AI developers, arguing that copying their work to build a competing product amounts to infringement on an industrial scale.
The developers' defense rests largely on the American doctrine of fair use, which permits certain unlicensed uses of copyrighted material if the new use is transformative rather than a mere substitute for the original. A model, they argue, does not store and resell books or pictures. It extracts statistical patterns from them, much as a human student assimilates a style by reading widely. Creators retort that the analogy is ____. A student cannot read millions of books in a month, and a student's essays do not inundate the market that sustains the student's teachers.
Early rulings have pointed in divergent directions. Some judges have treated training as transformative but stressed that illegally obtained copies or outputs reproducing protected passages nearly word for word may still expose companies to liability. Meanwhile many developers have begun signing licensing deals with publishers and image libraries, a sign that they regard paying for data as cheaper than prolonged litigation. Whatever the courts finally decide, the disputes have forced an old question into a new form: when a machine learns from human work, what, if anything, does it owe the people who made it?

Heat is often called a silent killer, and nowhere is it quieter than on a construction site or a farm. Unlike floods, a heat wave leaves no visible wreckage, yet it can be just as lethal for people who must keep working through it. As 2024 became the hottest year on record worldwide, protecting outdoor workers moved toward the center of labor policy.
When the air is both hot and humid, sweat evaporates sluggishly and the body's internal temperature climbs. Early symptoms such as dizziness are easily dismissed by laborers paid by the piece or anxious about forfeiting a day's wages, and by the time collapse occurs it may be too late. Several governments now mandate rest breaks in the shade once temperatures pass a certain threshold. But enforcement is another matter. Inspectors are scarce, and on a site racing to meet a deadline a compulsory break can quietly <u>fall by the wayside</u>.

The summer I turned nineteen, I set out to travel alone through the mountains of a country whose language I could barely read. On the fourth day I misread a timetable and arrived at a village bus stop twenty minutes after the last bus of the evening had departed. The road was empty, the light was fading, and my phone was dead because I had forgotten to charge it. I remember checking the timetable again and again, as if the numbers might rearrange themselves in my favor, while my heart pounded and every rustle in the trees sounded ominous.
A light was still on in a tiny shop across the road. The elderly woman inside scrutinized my face, my backpack, and the useless timetable in my hand and seemed to grasp my predicament without a word. She sat me down beside a kerosene heater, poured me a bowl of barley tea, and made a telephone call. Half an hour later her nephew arrived in a battered truck and drove me to the nearest town, declining the money I tried to press into his hand. By the time I reached my guesthouse the panic had drained out of me, leaving only a warm and slightly dazed gratitude.
I never learned the woman's name, and I could not find the village again on any map. Perhaps that is why the evening has stayed with me. A kindness that cannot be repaid to the giver has to go somewhere else, so for twenty years now I have been <u>settling the account with strangers</u>: giving directions, lending a charger, waiting with someone at a station until their ride appears.

In 1912 a German meteorologist named Alfred Wegener proposed an idea that most geologists of his day regarded as little short of absurd: the continents had once been joined in a single landmass and had slowly drifted apart over millions of years.
(A) The objection that proved decisive was not about his evidence but about his explanation. Wegener could not offer a cogent account of what force might push entire continents through the solid rock of the ocean floor, and the mechanisms he posited were shown to be woefully inadequate. Without a mechanism, critics concluded, drift was ____, a story that fit the facts too neatly to be trusted. By the time Wegener died on an expedition to Greenland in 1930, his theory had few defenders.
(B) The vindication came from a place Wegener could never have examined. After the Second World War, surveys of the ocean floor revealed a vast underwater mountain chain running down the middle of the Atlantic and symmetrical stripes of magnetized rock on either side of it. New crust was continually forming at such ridges and spreading outward, carrying the continents with it. By the late 1960s, the theory of plate tectonics had absorbed Wegener's central claim, and drift became textbook orthodoxy.
(C) His evidence was varied and, in hindsight, compelling: the coastlines of South America and Africa fit together like pieces of a puzzle. Fossils of the same ancient plants and reptiles turned up on continents now separated by thousands of kilometers of ocean, creatures that could hardly have swum across. Rock formations and the traces of ancient glaciers likewise appeared to match on opposite sides of the Atlantic.

When Samuel Johnson published his Dictionary of the English Language in 1755, many readers hoped it would do for English what academies in France and Italy had attempted for their own languages: fix it in a correct and permanent form. Johnson had begun with similar ambitions, but by the time he finished he had largely abandoned them. In his preface he conceded that no dictionary could stop a living language from changing, since words shift with the habits of those who use them.
That admission foreshadowed a profound change in how dictionaries are made. In the following century, the editors of what became the Oxford English Dictionary set out not to legislate usage but to record it, enlisting hundreds of volunteer readers to mail in slips showing each word in context, and tracing how meanings had emerged, multiplied, and faded.
The descriptive approach did not end the quarrel; it moved it. When an American dictionary published in 1961 included informal words with few warnings about their status, critics accused its editors of abandoning standards altogether. A dictionary that records how people talk without saying how they ought to, they argued, has surrendered the only authority that makes it worth consulting. Defenders replied that a dictionary which ignores how millions actually speak is not guarding the language but misrepresenting it.
Both camps have a point, though not the one they usually press. The critics were right that speakers want guidance, especially in formal writing, and that a reference which offers none leaves them adrift. The defenders were right that guidance pretending usage never moves soon becomes obsolete. Modern lexicographers have settled on an uneasy compromise, describing usage faithfully while adding labels that flag words likely to raise eyebrows in a job application. The compromise works tolerably well, but it rests on a judgment the descriptive ideal was meant to avoid: someone must still decide which words deserve a warning.

In the 1790s the Italian scientist Lazzaro Spallanzani noticed something perplexing about bats. Blindfolded bats, and even bats whose eyes had been removed, could still fly through a darkened room strung with threads without colliding with them. Yet when their ears were plugged, they blundered helplessly into obstacles. Spallanzani concluded that bats somehow saw with their ears, but he could not explain how, and many contemporaries dismissed the idea as fanciful. The answer had to wait until the late 1930s, when the American researcher Donald Griffin used equipment able to detect sounds above the range of human hearing. He showed that bats emit rapid, high-pitched calls and listen for the echoes, a process he called echolocation.
By analyzing the returning echoes, a hunting bat can judge not only the distance to an insect but also its size, direction, and even the beating of its wings. As the bat closes in, its calls become faster and culminate in a rapid burst just before capture, which gives it continually updated information about its quarry.
But prey have not remained ____. Many moths have evolved ears attuned to bat calls, and when they detect an approaching bat they dive, loop, or drop toward the ground. Some tiger moths go further, producing ultrasonic clicks of their own that may startle bats, warn them that the moth tastes foul, or even jam their sonar. The result is an evolutionary arms race conducted entirely in sounds that humans cannot hear.
Remarkably, some blind people have taught themselves a version of the same skill, producing sharp tongue clicks and interpreting the faint echoes to sense the shape and position of nearby objects.

Before the railway, time was a local affair. Each town set its clocks by the sun, declaring noon when the sun stood highest overhead, and because the sun reaches that point later as one travels west, neighboring towns might differ by several minutes. For people who traveled no faster than a horse, the discrepancy hardly mattered.
The railways changed that. A train covering hundreds of kilometers in a day passed through dozens of local times, and timetables that tried to honor them all became nearly unintelligible. British companies began adopting a single standard based on Greenwich in the 1840s, and in 1883 the railroads of the United States and Canada replaced a patchwork of local times with a handful of zones. It is customary to tell this story as a triumph of reason over parochial confusion, and in one sense it was: confusion about the time on a single-track line could send two trains toward each other.
Yet the triumphal version omits who made the decision. The American zones were adopted by the railroads themselves, not by any legislature; Congress did not make standard time law until 1918. Some communities resented having their clocks dictated by distant companies, and a number of towns obstinately kept local time alongside the new standard for years. Critics grumbled that railway time served the convenience of commerce rather than the rhythms of nature. They were not wrong about whose convenience came first, even if their attachment to solar noon now seems quaint.
Within a generation the standardized hour had become so ____ that few people could imagine life without it, and the resistance was largely forgotten. That forgetting is itself instructive. Today our phones quietly synchronize with atomic clocks, and it is easy to assume that the time we take for granted is simply the time. It was, rather, a deliberate and contested invention, beneficial on the whole, but imposed before it was agreed to.

In April 1815 Mount Tambora on the Indonesian island of Sumbawa erupted in the most powerful volcanic explosion in recorded history. The blast killed tens of thousands of people nearby, but its effects reached much farther. Enormous quantities of sulfur gas rose into the upper atmosphere, where they formed a haze that Ⓐ<u>reflected</u> sunlight back into space. The following year, 1816, became known in Europe and North America as the Year Without a Summer. Snow fell in New England in June, harvests Ⓑ<u>failed</u> across much of Europe, and food prices soared. Unaware of any link between volcanoes and climate, people at the time found the strange weather Ⓒ<u>unsurprising</u>. Today scientists regard the episode as a Ⓓ<u>sobering</u> illustration of how a single eruption can disrupt the global climate, a lesson they consider Ⓔ<u>relevant</u> to modern proposals to cool the planet artificially.

In college I took lecture notes on a laptop because I could type far Ⓐ<u>faster</u> than I could write, yet speed may not be an Ⓑ<u>advantage</u>. In several studies, students who typed could keep Ⓒ<u>pace</u> with the lecturer and reproduce what was said nearly word for word. In other words, they tended to Ⓓ<u>summarize</u> lectures rather than think about them. Those writing by hand could not keep up and were forced to condense what they heard into their own words, and this effort of selection and rephrasing appears to Ⓔ<u>deepen</u> understanding. When tested on the concepts later, hand-writers often performed as well as or better than typists. Later research has been mixed, but the findings suggest that the most efficient method of recording information is not always the most effective way of learning it.

Coral reefs owe their brilliant colors largely to microscopic algae that live inside the tissues of coral animals. The partnership is Ⓐ<u>mutually</u> beneficial: the algae receive shelter, and in return they supply the coral with most of the food it needs through photosynthesis. When ocean temperatures rise even a degree or two above normal for several weeks, however, this relationship breaks down. Stressed corals Ⓑ<u>retain</u> their algae, exposing their white skeletons, a process known as bleaching. Bleached corals are not yet dead, and if the water cools quickly they can Ⓒ<u>recover</u>. But prolonged heat leaves them Ⓓ<u>starving</u> and vulnerable to disease. As marine heat waves have grown more frequent, scientists worry that reefs are being given ever less time to recuperate between episodes, rendering their long-term survival increasingly Ⓔ<u>precarious</u>.

Scientific journals have long favored studies with striking, positive results: a drug that works, an effect that appears. Studies that find nothing are often rejected or never submitted, consigned to what researchers ruefully call the file drawer. The consequences are easy to underestimate. If twenty teams test an ineffective treatment, one may obtain a positive result by chance alone; if only that study reaches print, the literature will proclaim an effect that does not exist, and later reviews that pool the published evidence will merely compound the error.
Defenders of current practice offer an argument that deserves a hearing. A null result, they point out, is frequently not evidence of absence but merely absence of evidence: a study too small to detect a real effect will "find nothing" as reliably as one testing a genuinely useless drug. Editors who decline such work are not suppressing the truth, on this view, but sparing readers a flood of inconclusive noise. There is something to this. Many unpublished null studies are indeed underpowered, and a literature crowded with them would be harder, not easier, to read.
Yet the argument proves less than it seems to. It justifies rejecting poorly designed studies, whatever their results, not rejecting null results as such. A well-designed trial that finds no effect is as informative as one that finds a large effect, and arguably more so if it corrects a popular belief. This is why the most promising reforms judge a study before anyone knows its outcome. Some journals now commit to publishing a study on the basis of its design and methods, and many funders require that clinical trials be registered in advance, so that their disappearance would be conspicuous. Such measures will not empty the file drawer entirely. But they shift the question editors ask from whether a study found something to whether it was capable of finding anything.

The decipherment of Egyptian hieroglyphs is usually told as the triumph of a single mind. For centuries scholars had assumed that the symbols were purely pictorial, each standing for an idea rather than a sound, and their attempts at translation produced little more than fanciful guesses. Then, in 1822, the young Frenchman Jean-François Champollion announced that hieroglyphs combined phonetic signs with symbols for whole words, and three thousand years of Egyptian history became readable almost overnight.
Historians of the decipherment have grown wary of this tidy narrative. The key that made the breakthrough possible, a stone slab found near Rosetta in 1799 bearing the same decree in hieroglyphic, demotic, and Greek, had been studied by others for two decades. The English polymath Thomas Young had already identified several phonetic signs in the royal names enclosed in oval rings, and Champollion, a fierce rival, was slow to acknowledge the debt. On this account, Champollion was less a lone discoverer than the fortunate heir of a collective effort, whose fame owes as much to national pride as to originality.
The corrective is useful, but it can be pressed too far. Young believed that phonetic signs were used only for foreign names, a special device for spelling words the script could not otherwise express; he never abandoned the assumption that native Egyptian words were written in pictures. Champollion's decisive step was to show that the same principle ran through the entire writing system, and he could take it because, unlike Young, he had mastered Coptic, the late form of the Egyptian language, which allowed him to hear the words the signs were spelling. Inheritance, in other words, explains where he started, not where he arrived. The breakthrough was built on shared foundations, but the building was largely his.

The axolotl, a salamander native to the lakes and canals around Mexico City, occupies a peculiar position among endangered animals. In the wild it is nearly gone, its numbers collapsed by pollution, urban expansion, and introduced fish. In laboratories and home aquariums around the world, by contrast, it is abundant: its capacity to regrow limbs, parts of its spinal cord, and even portions of its heart has made it a favorite of researchers studying tissue repair, and its perpetually youthful appearance has made it a popular pet. It is tempting to conclude that the species is in no real danger, since it could always be returned to the wild from the tanks in which it already thrives.
There is a grain of truth in this. Captive breeding has rescued other species, and the axolotl's willingness to reproduce in captivity is an asset many conservationists would envy. But the comfort is largely illusory. Most laboratory axolotls descend from a few dozen animals shipped to Paris in the nineteenth century, and some lines were later crossed with a related species of salamander to introduce useful traits. Generations of life in still, clean, temperate water have also favored animals suited to tanks rather than to canals full of predators and fluctuating temperatures. What survives in captivity, then, is not quite the animal that is disappearing from Mexico.
None of this makes captive stocks worthless. They preserve a great deal of the species' biology, and they may yet prove indispensable if the wild population vanishes altogether. The lesson is rather that they cannot substitute for the habitat. Some of the most hopeful efforts in Mexico involve farmers who maintain traditional plots in the canals, filtering the water and excluding invasive fish, so that wild axolotls can persist where they evolved. An ark is a fine thing to have, but no one should mistake it for dry land.

In 1999 the psychologists David Dunning and Justin Kruger reported that people who performed worst on tests of logic, grammar, and humor tended to overestimate their abilities dramatically: those scoring near the bottom often rated themselves above average. The researchers proposed that the least competent are doubly handicapped. Because the skills needed to perform well in a domain are often the very skills needed to recognize good performance, such people not only err but also fail to perceive their errors. The idea spread far beyond psychology, and the "Dunning-Kruger effect" became a popular shorthand for the confident ignorance of others.
Some statisticians have since argued that much of the pattern requires no psychological explanation at all. Almost everyone rates themselves somewhat above average, and self-ratings are only loosely tied to actual scores. Under those two conditions, the lowest scorers will inevitably appear to overestimate themselves most, and the highest scorers to underestimate themselves, even if no one's self-insight differs from anyone else's. Simulations using random numbers in place of self-assessments can reproduce the famous graph with unsettling fidelity.
This critique is a serious one, and it ought to temper the enthusiasm with which the effect is invoked. It does not, however, dispose of the original idea. Studies designed to separate genuine misjudgment from statistical noise have generally found that poor performers do judge their own performance less accurately than strong performers, though the gap is considerably smaller than the striking early graphs implied. What emerges is a modest tendency rather than a law of human nature. There is an irony here worth noting: the effect is most often cited by people confident that it describes someone else, which is perhaps the best reason to hold one's own certainty about it more loosely.

For decades cities competed fiercely for tourists, treating every additional visitor as a welcome boost to local prosperity, but in many destinations that consensus is fraying. Residents of popular old towns lament that short-term rentals have driven up rents and hollowed out neighborhoods. Bakeries and hardware stores have given way to souvenir shops, and narrow streets become nearly impassable in peak season. In the summer of 2024 demonstrators in Barcelona marched through tourist districts, and some squirted visitors with water pistols to dramatize their exasperation.
Authorities have begun to experiment with ways of taming the crowds. In 2024 Venice became the first major city to charge day-trippers an entry fee, initially five euros on the busiest days. Japan introduced a fee and a daily cap for climbers on the most popular trail up Mount Fuji. Elsewhere cities have curbed new holiday rentals, restricted large tour groups, or raised levies on overnight stays. The rationale is straightforward: when visitors impose costs on residents beyond the price of a trip, a charge can make them ____ part of this burden.
Skeptics doubt that such measures will accomplish much, for a fee of a few euros is negligible compared with the cost of flights and hotels, and few economists expect so modest a charge to deter many visitors. Some suspect that officials are merely dressing up a revenue grab as crowd control. Others worry that steep charges could turn historic centers into playgrounds reserved for the affluent.
Still, the debate marks a notable shift, as tourism is increasingly regarded not as an unalloyed blessing but as a resource like water or road space, to be rationed when demand outstrips supply.

Beneath the floor of a forest lies a network that few visitors ever contemplate. The roots of most trees are colonized by fungi whose threadlike filaments ramify through the soil, absorbing water and minerals for the trees in exchange for sugars. A single fungus can attach to the roots of several trees at once, so scientists realized that trees might be linked through these subterranean threads in a web that journalists soon nicknamed the wood wide web.
The idea captivated the public imagination, and popular books and documentaries portrayed forests as cooperative communities in which venerable mother trees nourish their seedlings, send carbon to struggling neighbors, and warn one another of insect attacks through chemical signals traveling along the fungal network. Forests, in this telling, were less an aggregate of competing individuals than a kind of society.
In recent years, however, a number of researchers have urged caution. Reviewing the field in 2023, a group of ecologists argued that the evidence for some of the most popular claims is far thinner than public enthusiasm suggests. They acknowledged that shared networks clearly exist. But experiments showing meaningful transfers of resources between trees, with real benefits to the receiving tree, are scarce and often amenable to other interpretations. Many studies, they noted, had been cited in ways that went well beyond what their authors had found.
None of this means that the underground world is unimportant. Fungi are indispensable to the health of forests. The lesson, the skeptics suggest, and it is a sound one, is that a vivid story can ____ the data on which it rests and that scientists must take care not to let a seductive metaphor supplant evidence.

Short-form video has become the lingua franca of the smartphone. Platforms built around clips lasting seconds rather than minutes now attract well over a billion users, and older services have hurried to emulate the format. Their allure is not hard to fathom: each swipe offers something new, and recommendation algorithms learn with uncanny speed which clips will keep a particular viewer watching.
Critics worry that this endless novelty exacts a price. The next reward is always a flick of the thumb away, so heavy users may grow impatient with anything that demands sustained effort, from a long novel to an intricate lecture. As a teacher I watch students struggle to sit through a full-length film without reaching for their phones, and I confess to finding it harder to immerse myself in a book than I once did.
But the scientific evidence is less conclusive than the anecdotes. Studies have found correlations between heavy short-video use and weaker self-reported attention, but most are surveys taken at a single point in time, which cannot establish what causes what. People who already find concentration arduous may simply gravitate toward rapid, easily digested content. Researchers also note that the shrinking attention span has been blamed in turn on television, video games, and the early internet.
What seems clearer is that attention behaves less like a fixed capacity than like a habit. Tasks we practice become easier, while those we shun grow more daunting. A reader who fills every idle moment with scrolling is not necessarily losing the ability to focus, but may be ____ it, much as an unused muscle atrophies without disappearing.

"Every page," Mrs. Okafor said, tapping the lid of a cardboard box. "We read every page before anything goes." She was a retired seamstress from two doors down, and my mother had arranged for me to help her sort through her late husband's study during my school vacation. I agreed only for the promised pay and arrived on the first morning determined to finish as expeditiously as possible. The room was crammed with boxes of letters, receipts, and notebooks, and she meant exactly what she had said. By the third day I was openly sulking, sighing theatrically whenever she lingered over a faded envelope.
On the fourth afternoon she handed me a notebook and asked me to read it aloud, since her eyes tired easily. It turned out to be a diary her husband had kept during his first year in this country, when he worked nights in a bakery and slept in a rented room he shared with two strangers. He wrote about the cold, about money, about missing his mother's voice. Then, on a page dated in early spring, he described meeting a young woman at a bus stop who had laughed at his dreadful joke. Mrs. Okafor said nothing, but when I looked up she was smiling with her eyes closed.
I did not sulk again that summer. I began to understand that we were not clearing out a room but <u>listening to a life</u>, and that the slowness I had resented was a form of reverence. She later gave me the diary's last page, which still hangs in a frame above my desk.

The electric car is often marketed as a clean machine, but it depends on a long and frequently grimy supply chain. Its battery requires lithium, nickel, cobalt, graphite, and other minerals. These must be extracted, refined, and assembled into cells before a single vehicle leaves the factory. As sales of electric vehicles have climbed, governments have begun to regard this chain less as a matter of commerce than as one of national security.
The anxiety stems from concentration: a large share of the world's cobalt is mined in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, often under conditions criticized trenchantly by human-rights groups. China dominates the refining of many battery minerals and the manufacture of the cells themselves. Countries hoping to build battery industries of their own therefore find themselves dependent on a ____ that is also a strategic rival. In ordinary times such reliance may seem a reasonable bargain, since Chinese producers have invested heavily and offer low prices. In a crisis, critics warn, it could prove a crippling vulnerability.
In response the United States, the European Union, and others have offered generous subsidies to encourage mining, refining, and battery production at home or among trusted partners. Skeptics note that these policies can raise costs for consumers and provoke disputes with trading partners and that new mines and refineries take many years to build amid fierce local opposition over pollution and water use. A mine approved today may not yield ore until the next decade.
Engineers, meanwhile, are attacking the problem from another direction. Batteries based on lithium iron phosphate require no cobalt or nickel and have rapidly gained market share, and researchers are developing sodium-ion cells that dispense with lithium altogether. Recycling may eventually supply a meaningful fraction of the minerals needed, as the first generation of electric cars reaches the scrapyard. None of these innovations will end the scramble for raw materials soon, but together they suggest that the map of dependence is not immutable.

Every flat map of the world is a compromise. It is impossible to press the curved surface of a globe flat without stretching or tearing it somewhere, so mapmakers must decide which properties to preserve and which to sacrifice. The projection published by the Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator in 1569 preserved angles: a line of constant compass bearing appeared on it as a straight line, so a navigator could plot a course with a ruler and hold a single heading. The price was a dramatic distortion of size toward the poles. Greenland appears roughly as large as Africa, although Africa is about fourteen times larger.
In the 1970s critics charged that the map was no innocent instrument. By shrinking the tropics and swelling the northern latitudes, they argued, it had taught generations of schoolchildren to see Europe as the center of the world and the global South as marginal, and they promoted an equal-area alternative that restored the continents to their true proportions. The map's popularity in classrooms, on this account, was itself evidence of the worldview it served.
The charge contains an important truth, but it misplaces the blame. Mercator's distortions follow from geometry, not from prejudice: any projection that keeps angles true must enlarge high latitudes, and the same mathematics swells Antarctica and Siberia, regions few Europeans of his day had any wish to glorify. What deserves criticism is less the design than its use, for a chart built for sailors was hung on classroom walls where no one needed to steer a ship. Nor did the proposed remedy escape the problem it diagnosed. The equal-area map kept sizes honest only by stretching shapes, so that Africa appeared elongated and narrow, a distortion of a different kind. The lesson is not that one projection is ideological and another neutral, but that each embodies a judgment, and that the judgment should fit the purpose.

In a widely cited experiment published in 2000, researchers set up a tasting table in an upscale grocery store that displayed either six varieties of jam or twenty-four. The larger display drew more visitors, yet shoppers who had seen only six flavors were far more likely to buy a jar. The finding gave scientific respectability to a suspicion many people already held: beyond a certain point, adding options does not liberate consumers but leaves them paralyzed, anxious about choosing wrongly and less satisfied with whatever they finally select. Retailers pruned their product lines, and advisers urged that retirement plans offer fewer funds.
The idea seemed to overturn a cherished tenet of economics, namely that more choice can never make a rational person worse off, since one can always ignore the superfluous options. Yet the economists' position was never quite as naive as its critics implied. Ignoring options is not free; it requires knowing which ones to ignore, and that knowledge is precisely what an overwhelmed shopper lacks. In this sense the jam study did not so much refute rational choice as remind economists that information has a cost.
Later research complicated the picture further. When psychologists pooled the results of dozens of studies, the average effect of large assortments turned out to be close to zero: abundant choice sometimes discouraged decisions, sometimes had no effect, and sometimes helped. Overload appeared mainly when people lacked clear preferences, when options were hard to compare, and when the decision had to be made in haste. It would be wrong to conclude that choice overload is a myth; under the right conditions it is real enough. But it is a property of how options are presented and of who is choosing, not of the sheer number of options. The practical lesson for designers of menus and public programs is therefore less to cut than to organize.

For decades physicists have quipped that a working fusion reactor is perpetually three decades off. Fusion powers the sun and releases prodigious amounts of energy when light atomic nuclei are forced together. On Earth it requires heating fuel to many millions of degrees and confining it long enough for reactions to occur. The task is so formidable that no experiment had ever produced more energy from its fuel than was delivered to it.
That changed in December 2022. Scientists at a national laboratory in California fired powerful lasers at a tiny fuel capsule and for the first time obtained more fusion energy than the lasers had deposited in the target. The feat was hailed as historic but came with <u>an important asterisk</u>: the facility as a whole consumed far more electricity to power its lasers than the reaction released, so the experiment was a scientific milestone rather than a practical source of power.
Since then enthusiasm has spread beyond government laboratories. Private fusion companies have raised billions of dollars, and some technology firms anxious about the voracious electricity demands of their data centers have signed agreements to buy power from fusion plants that do not yet exist. Meanwhile the international ITER project in southern France, intended to demonstrate fusion on an industrial scale, has suffered repeated delays and cost overruns.
Skeptics point out that daunting engineering obstacles remain, from materials that can withstand relentless bombardment by neutrons to the challenge of producing fuel. Even optimists concede that fusion is unlikely to contribute much to curbing emissions in the coming decade, the very period of greatest urgency for the transition away from fossil fuels. Wind, solar power, and batteries, already cheap and proven, must shoulder this burden.

An ancient puzzle recorded by Plutarch concerns the ship of Theseus, which the Athenians preserved for centuries by replacing each decaying plank with a new one. Once every original plank was gone, was it still the same ship? And if someone had gathered the discarded planks and reassembled them, which vessel would have the stronger claim? Philosophers have long treated the riddle as a test of what identity consists in, and two answers have dominated. One holds that identity follows material: the reassembled planks are the true ship. The other holds that it follows continuity of form and function: the ship that kept sailing, however rebuilt, remains Theseus's.
Each answer, pressed hard, yields absurdities. If identity follows material, then a person whose cells have all been replaced is a stranger to her childhood self; if it follows continuity alone, then a museum could replace every brushstroke of a painting and still claim to display the original. Some philosophers conclude from such cases that the question is simply empty, a quarrel about words with no fact to be discovered. That conclusion is tempting, and it may even be correct about the ship. It is harder to sustain once something depends on the answer. Courts must decide whether an offender convicted decades after a crime is truly the person who committed it, and conservators must judge how much of an old temple can be renewed before it becomes a replica of itself. What such cases suggest is that identity is less a fact waiting to be discovered than a ____ guided by what we have reason to value. The conservator who prizes original material and the one who prizes a living tradition of rebuilding are not disagreeing about planks or stones. When the Electronic Numerical Integrator and Computer, better known as ENIAC, was unveiled to the press in 1946, newspapers marveled at a machine capable of thousands of calculations a second. Built at the University of Pennsylvania to compute artillery firing tables for the U.S. Army, it filled a large room, contained some eighteen thousand vacuum tubes, and devoured prodigious amounts of electricity. The engineers who designed its circuitry were lionized as pioneers. Far less attention went to the small team of women who had worked out how to make it do anything at all.
ENIAC could not Ⓐ<u>store</u> programs in the modern sense. To tackle a new problem, operators had to Ⓑ<u>rewire</u> it by hand, plugging cables and setting thousands of switches according to diagrams of their own design, often with little more than the machine's blueprints to guide them. The work demanded Ⓒ<u>formidable</u> mathematical skill and an intimate grasp of the hardware, since a single misplaced cable could vitiate an entire calculation. Yet at the time, programming was widely regarded as Ⓓ<u>prestigious</u> clerical work, a mere extension of the hand computation that women had long performed for the military. In publicity photographs, the women frequently went unidentified, treated as little more than <u>part of the scenery</u>.
Only decades later did historians begin to Ⓔ<u>recover</u> their story, interviewing the surviving programmers and restoring their names to the record. Their belated recognition illustrates a recurrent pattern in the history of technology: the prestige of a task often depends less on its intrinsic difficulty than on who happens to perform it. Once programming came to be seen as intellectually demanding and lucrative, it was gradually redefined as a predominantly male profession and the contributions of its earliest practitioners receded from view.
